                    ### Question
                    A 3-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of recurrent nosebleeds and fatigue for the past 2 months. He also frequently complains his head hurts. The patient has met all motoric milestones for his age but does not like to run because his legs start to hurt if he does. He is at the 40th percentile for both height and weight. His temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 125/min, respirations are 32/min, and blood pressure in the right arm is 130/85 mm Hg. A grade 2/6 systolic murmur is heard in the left paravertebral region. Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Inferior rib notching
opb. Interarm difference in tissue oxygenation
opc. Pulmonary valve stenosis
opd. Left-axis deviation on ECG
ope. Delayed pulse in lower extremities

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The 3-year-old boy's symptoms of recurrent nosebleeds, fatigue, headaches, and leg pain during running, combined with elevated blood pressure (130/85 mm Hg) in the upper body, suggest a diagnosis of coarctation of the aorta. This condition can lead to collateral circulation, which is indicated by the systolic murmur in the left paravertebral region. Inferior rib notching is a classic finding associated with long-standing coarctation due to erosion of the ribs by collateral circulation. The possibility of an interarm difference in tissue oxygenation is also relevant, as coarctation can lead to differential blood flow. However, pulmonary valve stenosis is unlikely given the context, and left-axis deviation on ECG is not a primary finding in this case. Delayed pulse in the lower extremities is consistent with coarctation. Therefore, the most likely finding upon further evaluation is inferior rib notching.
